notes.h: Criteria for selecting materials (Higher Level only)
notes.b: No material is best for everything, so each one is judged against how the room is used and what the household needs before it is chosen. These criteria give you a checklist for justifying any choice.
points: Durability: resistance to wear, impact, moisture and heat determines how long a material will last in a given room, so a kitchen worktop needs much more than a bedroom shelf.
Cost: the purchase price, fitting costs and upkeep over the life of the material all count, because a cheap material that needs replacing often can cost more in the end.
Appearance and texture: the material must suit the style, colour scheme and décor of the room.
Ease of cleaning and maintenance: non-porous, sealed or washable materials need less upkeep because dirt and spills do not soak in.
Safety in use: slip resistance on floors, safe edges on furniture and toughened or laminated glass where people could be injured.
Insulation: poor conductors such as wood, plastics and fabric feel warmer to touch and reduce heat loss; good conductors such as metal feel cold.
Environmental impact: the source of the material, how far it travels, whether it can be recycled and how long it lasts.
Suitability for the job: the material must have the strength and the resistance to water and heat that its use demands.
notes.tip: Questions can name a use, such as a kitchen worktop, a bathroom window or child's furniture. Justify your material choice with the criteria: durability, cost, safety, ease of cleaning, insulation and environmental impact.

notes.h: Solid woods: hardwoods and softwoods (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Wood is a natural material used for many parts of the home, from floors to furniture. Solid woods fall into two groups, hardwoods and softwoods, which differ in cost, durability and use.
points: Solid hardwoods such as ash, beech, elm, oak, mahogany, rosewood and walnut are expensive, durable and resistant to decay and warping, and they have an attractive grain.
Solid hardwoods are used for floors, stairs, furniture, doors, architraves (the decorative frames around doors), windows, skirting boards and decking.

Softwoods such as pine and spruce (also called deal) are cheaper and easier to work, but they dent and scratch more readily than hardwoods. They are used for floorboards, joists, roof timbers, doors, windows, furniture and shelving.
Hardwood and softwood describe the type of tree, not how hard the wood is. Hardwoods are usually denser and more durable, but not every hardwood is harder than every softwood.
Example of one solid wood: oak is a hardwood that is hard-wearing, durable and expensive, and it is used for floors, stairs and furniture.
notes.tip: If asked to describe one solid wood, name a single wood such as oak or beech and say it is a hardwood. Give its properties (durable, resistant to decay and warping, expensive) and at least two uses. Do not offer MDF or chipboard, because they are manufactured boards, not solid wood.

notes.h: Wood as a natural material: seasoning and protection (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Because wood comes from a living tree, it keeps reacting to its surroundings after it is cut. This is why it needs preparation and a protective finish.
points: Wood is a natural material that shrinks, swells and warps with changes in humidity, so it must be well seasoned (dried) before use.
Varnish, lacquer or sealant protects wood from moisture and wear and keeps its surface easy to clean. Stain or paint can be used for the same protection.
Wood is a poor conductor of heat, so it feels warm to touch.
Wood is renewable if it is sustainably sourced, which helps its environmental impact.

notes.h: Manufactured boards: veneer, plywood, MDF and chipboard (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Solid wood is expensive, so wood is also made into boards. These give a large, stable surface at lower cost, and they are manufactured boards, not solid wood.
points: Veneer is a thin layer of attractive hardwood glued over a cheaper core, giving the look of solid wood at lower cost.
Plywood is made of thin wood layers glued together with the grain of each layer at right angles to the next, which makes it strong, stable and resistant to warping.
Medium-density fibreboard (MDF) is made from wood fibres bonded with resin; it has a smooth surface that takes paint well but swells if it gets wet.
Chipboard is made from wood chips bonded with resin; it is cheap and widely used for kitchen units and flooring, but it is weak when wet.
notes.tip: Remember that moisture is the weakness of MDF and chipboard, so link them to dry uses and give water damage as their disadvantage.

notes.b: Metals are chosen where strength, heat conduction or a hygienic surface matter most. Each metal has its own strengths, which decide where it is used in the home.
points: Metals used in the home include steel, stainless steel, aluminium, copper, brass and cast iron.
Metals are strong and hard-wearing, and they are good conductors of heat and electricity, which is why they feel cold to touch.
Ordinary steel rusts unless it is coated or painted; stainless steel contains chromium, which resists corrosion, so it is hygienic and easy to keep clean.
Stainless steel is used for sinks, worktops, cooker hoods and appliance fronts in kitchens, and for cutlery.
Aluminium is lightweight and resists corrosion because it forms a protective oxide layer; it is used for window frames, saucepans and fittings.
Copper is malleable (easily shaped) and a good conductor, so it is used for hot water pipes, cylinders and saucepan bases.
Brass is an alloy (a mixture of metals) of copper and zinc that resists corrosion and is used for taps, door handles and other decorative fittings.
Cast iron is heavy and brittle and retains heat; it is used for fireplaces, radiators and cooking pots.
notes.tip: If asked for a metal for a given fitting, name the metal, give the property that suits the job (for example, stainless steel resists corrosion, so it suits sinks) and name the use.

notes.b: Glass lets light into a room while keeping weather out, and its surface is easy to keep clean. Its brittleness and its poor heat retention when used as a single pane are why special types of glass are made.
points: Glass is made mainly from sand heated with other materials.
It is transparent, non-porous, hygienic and easy to clean, and it is hard but brittle.
Single glazing loses heat easily, whereas double glazing traps a layer of air or argon and reduces heat loss.

notes.h: Types of glass and their uses (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Plain glass breaks into sharp pieces and lets heat escape, so different types have been developed to make glass safer, warmer or more private.
points: Float glass is smooth and clear and is the basic glass used in windows and in mirrors, which are made by coating it with a reflective layer.

Toughened glass is heat treated so that it shatters into small blunt pieces when broken and withstands heat and stress better; it is used for shower screens, glass doors, low-level glazing and oven doors.
Laminated glass is two sheets bonded with a plastic interlayer, so that it holds together when broken and resists break-ins; it is used for windscreens and security glazing.
Double glazing has two panes with a sealed gap of air or argon, which reduces heat loss and noise.
Low-emissivity (low-E) glass has a thin coating that reduces heat escaping through the window while still letting in light.
Frosted or patterned glass lets light through while obscuring the view, which suits bathrooms and hall doors.
Glass bricks refract light, bending it as it passes through, and let light through partitions and walls; frosted glass diffuses light so that it spreads evenly across the room.
notes.tip: Glass could be asked about for a stated use, such as a bathroom window or a shower screen. Match the type to the need: toughened for safety, laminated for security, double glazing for warmth and quiet, frosted for privacy.

notes.b: Plastics are moulded into many household items. They fall into two groups, thermoplastic and thermosetting, that behave very differently when heated.
points: Plastics are made from polymers, which are long chains of molecules, usually from petroleum.
They are lightweight, waterproof, easy to clean and easily coloured and moulded, and they are poor conductors of heat and electricity.
notes.tip: Students often reverse the two groups. Thermoplastic means softens with heat; thermosetting means sets hard and stays hard.

notes.b: A thermoplastic can be softened by heat again and again, like wax, which makes it easy to shape but means it cannot take high temperatures.
points: Thermoplastics are soft and flexible, soften when heated, can be moulded and remoulded, and harden again when cooled.
They are damaged by solvents but not by most acids and alkalis.
Polyethylene is a thermoplastic used for bottles, food containers, toys and bowls.
PTFE, also called Teflon, is a fluorocarbon thermoplastic with a non-stick finish used on saucepans and frying pans, and it is still classed as thermoplastic even though it tolerates cooking heat.
Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) is a thermoplastic used for vinyl floor and wall coverings, pipes and window frames.
notes.tip: Differentiating the two types is the most reliably repeated item. Use three headings (properties, examples, uses), with two properties and two named examples with a use for each type. A two-column table is the best revision form.

notes.b: A thermosetting plastic sets permanently the first time it is moulded, like a baked cake that cannot be melted back into batter. This is why it can withstand high temperatures.
points: Thermosetting plastics are hard and rigid and cannot be remoulded once set; they withstand high temperatures but blister and crack if overheated.
Thermosetting plastics are damaged by strong acids and alkalis but not by solvents, the opposite of thermoplastics.
Melamine formaldehyde is a thermosetting plastic used for cups, plates, saucers and laminated worktops.
Phenol formaldehyde is a thermosetting plastic used for the interior paddles of top-loading washing machines.
Bakelite is a thermosetting plastic used for light switches, telephones, utensil handles and cooker control knobs.
notes.tip: Chemical resistance runs opposite ways: thermoplastics are damaged by solvents, thermosetting plastics by strong acids and alkalis. Thermosetting plastics withstand high temperatures; thermoplastics do not. List Bakelite as a separate example with its own uses.

notes.h: Fabric: where it is used and what to look for (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Fabrics soften and decorate a home, and each use puts different demands on the material. Judge a fabric by the same kind of criteria as any other material.
points: Fabrics in the home are used for curtains, upholstery, carpets, bed linen and cushions.
Criteria for choosing a fabric are durability, drape (how it hangs), colour fastness and fade resistance, cleanability, flame resistance, comfort and cost.
Upholstery fabric should be durable, comfortable, resilient, stain resistant, hard-wearing and fire resistant.
Woven fabrics are stable and strong, while knitted fabrics stretch and recover their shape.
notes.tip: If asked for a fabric for upholstery or curtains, match its properties to the use and the criteria, such as durability, cleanability and fade resistance.

notes.b: Natural fibres come from plants and animals. Each has a typical set of strengths and weaknesses.
points: Cotton is absorbent and washable, and it is cool, but it creases easily and shrinks unless it is pre-shrunk.
Linen is strong and absorbent and feels cool to touch, but it creases easily.
Wool is warm, resilient and insulating, but it can shrink or felt if washed incorrectly.
Silk is soft and lustrous and drapes well, but it is delicate and expensive.

notes.h: Man-made fibres, velvet and blends (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Man-made fibres are manufactured to give properties that natural fibres lack, such as crease resistance and strength.
points: Polyester is strong, resists creasing and dries quickly, and it is often blended with cotton to combine comfort and durability.
Nylon is very strong and resists abrasion, which makes it suitable for carpets and upholstery that receive heavy wear.
Acrylic is a man-made fibre that feels like wool, takes bright colours and resists fading in sunlight.
Velvet is a pile fabric made from several fibres, not a man-made fibre.
Blends combine the advantages of each fibre, so one fibre's weakness is covered by another's strength.

keyTerms.definition: A plastic that softens when heated, can be moulded and remoulded, and hardens again when it cools.
A plastic that sets hard on first moulding and cannot be softened and remoulded by heating.
A material made of long chains of repeated molecular units, from which plastics and many fibres are made.
Glass that has been heat treated to shatter into small blunt pieces when broken, making it safer than ordinary glass.
Two sheets of glass bonded with a plastic interlayer so that the glass holds together when broken.
Glass with a thin coating that reduces the heat escaping through a window while still letting light through.
A thin layer of attractive hardwood glued over a cheaper core material.
A manufactured board made from wood chips bonded with resin, which is cheap but weak when wet.
A steel containing chromium that resists corrosion and is easy to keep hygienic.

questions.prompt: Identify two thermoplastics used in the home and state one property of each.
questions.model: Two thermoplastics identified, 1 mark each (for example polyethylene, PTFE or PVC). Property of each stated, 2 marks each: softens when heated and can be moulded and remoulded; hardens again on cooling. Non-stick finish for PTFE, flexible and resistant to acids and alkalis for PVC, or lightweight and used for food containers for polyethylene, as applicable.

questions.prompt: A householder is choosing materials for two items: a kitchen storage unit and a fitted wardrobe in a bedroom. Compare the suitability of solid hardwood and a manufactured board for each item, justifying your choice with reference to durability, resistance to moisture, cost and appearance.
questions.model: Kitchen storage unit (up to 12 marks): a manufactured board such as plywood or moisture-resistant board is suitable for a unit that carries a load and is exposed to moisture; plywood is strong and stable, while chipboard is cheap but weak when wet and swells if water enters the joints, so it should be sealed or edged. Solid hardwood is durable and attractive but expensive and can warp in the humidity of a kitchen unless well seasoned and finished. Bedroom wardrobe (up to 12 marks): solid hardwood or veneered board gives a good appearance in a bedroom and suits a finished piece; solid hardwood resists warping and decay and is durable, but cost is high; MDF takes paint well for a smooth painted finish at lower cost but swells if it gets wet, which is less of a concern in a bedroom. The choice in each case is justified by the function and environment of the item.
